2. Pre-Jump ($y_1$) Profile Computation:
  • At any elevation $Z$ on the sloping glacis, available specific energy: $$E_1 = \text{U/S TEL} - Z = 261.06 - Z$$
  • Pre-jump depth $y_1$ satisfies the specific energy cubic: $$E_1 = y_1 + \frac{q^2}{2g y_1^2} = y_1 + \frac{(13.86)^2}{2 \times 9.81 \times y_1^2} = y_1 + \frac{9.79}{y_1^2}$$
  • At toe of glacis ($Z = 252.70\text{ m}$): $$E_1 = 261.06 - 252.70 = 8.36\text{ m}$$ $$8.36 = y_1 + \frac{9.79}{y_1^2} \implies y_1 \approx \mathbf{1.14\text{ m}}$$ $$V_1 = \frac{13.86}{1.14} = 12.16\text{ m/s} \implies Fr_1 = \frac{12.16}{\sqrt{9.81 \times 1.14}} = \frac{12.16}{3.344} = 3.64$$
  • At mid-glacis ($Z = 254.85\text{ m}$): $$E_1 = 261.06 - 254.85 = 6.21\text{ m} \implies y_1 \approx \mathbf{1.34\text{ m}}$$
3. Post-Jump ($y_2$) Sequent Depth & Profile Computation:
  • Using Belanger's equation for sequent depth $y_2$: $$y_2 = \frac{y_1}{2}\left(\sqrt{1 + 8 Fr_1^2} - 1\right)$$
  • At toe of glacis ($y_1 = 1.14\text{ m}, Fr_1 = 3.64$): $$y_2 = \frac{1.14}{2}\left(\sqrt{1 + 8(3.64)^2} - 1\right) = 0.57 \times (\sqrt{107.0} - 1) = 0.57 \times 9.34 = \mathbf{5.32\text{ m}}$$
  • Post-jump water level ($J_2C$) at toe of glacis: $$\text{Post-Jump Water Level} = Z + y_2 = 252.70 + 5.32 = \mathbf{258.02\text{ m}}$$
  • Downstream actual tailwater level = $259.27\text{ m}$
  • Since downstream water level ($259.27\text{ m}$) exceeds the post-jump water level ($258.02\text{ m}$), the jump is drowned at the toe and rides up the $3:1$ glacis.
4. Jump Location on Sloping Glacis:
  • The jump forms on the $3:1$ glacis where $Z + y_2 = \text{Tailwater Level} = 259.27\text{ m}$.
  • By linear interpolation along the $12.9\text{ m}$ glacis slope, the jump stabilizes at elevation $\approx 253.80\text{ m}$ (approx $3.3\text{ m}$ upstream of the toe).
  • Downstream floor length check: Length provided = $29.0\text{ m} > 5(y_2 - y_1) = 5(5.32 - 1.14) = 20.9\text{ m}$ (Adequate to contain the entire jump).

topic: Canal Fluming & Transitions: Mitra's & Chaturvedi's Methods
question:
Design the Contraction Transition for a Siphon Aqueduct using Hind's Method:

**Design Tasks:**
1. Channel fluming geometry (flumed width and length of transition).
2. Water surface and bed elevation transition equations.

**Given Channel & Flume Data:**
- Upstream Bed Width ($B_1$) = $20.00\text{ m}$ | Flumed Bed Width ($B_2$) = $10.00\text{ m}$
- Upstream Depth ($y_1$) = $2.00\text{ m}$ | Upstream Velocity ($v_1$) = $1.00\text{ m/s}$
solution:
1. Given Hydraulic Parameters at Entry and Exit:
  • At Entry Section (Normal Canal Section 1):
    • Bed width ($B_1$) = $18.0\text{ m}$; Side slope ($m$) = $1.5\text{H}:1\text{V}$
    • Water depth ($y_1$) = $3.0\text{ m}$ (Given); Velocity ($V_1$) = $2.12\text{ m/s}$ (Given)
    • Total Energy Level ($\text{TEL}_1$) = $152.73\text{ m}$ (Given)
    • Flow Area: $$A_1 = (B_1 + m y_1) y_1 = (18.0 + 1.5 \times 3.0) \times 3.0 = 22.5 \times 3.0 = \mathbf{67.50\text{ m}^2}$$
    • Discharge ($Q$): $$Q = A_1 V_1 = 67.50 \times 2.12 = \mathbf{143.10\text{ m}^3/\text{s}}$$
    • Velocity head ($h_{v1}$): $$h_{v1} = \frac{V_1^2}{2g} = \frac{(2.12)^2}{2 \times 9.81} = \frac{4.4944}{19.62} = \mathbf{0.229\text{ m}}$$
    • Water Surface Level ($\text{FSL}_1$): $$\text{FSL}_1 = \text{TEL}_1 - h_{v1} = 152.73 - 0.229 = \mathbf{152.501\text{ m}}$$
    • Bed Level at Entry = $\text{FSL}_1 - y_1 = 152.501 - 3.00 = \mathbf{149.501\text{ m}}$
  • At Exit Section (Aqueduct Flumed Throat Section 2):
    • Bed width ($B_2$) = $6.3\text{ m}$; Side slope = Vertical ($m = 0$)
    • Water depth ($y_2$) = $2.10\text{ m}$ (Given directly in question — no assumption required)
    • Velocity ($V_2$) = $1.0\text{ m/s}$ (Given); Total Energy Level ($\text{TEL}_2$) = $152.77\text{ m}$ (Given)
    • Flow Area: $$A_2 = B_2 \times y_2 = 6.30 \times 2.10 = \mathbf{13.23\text{ m}^2}$$
    • Velocity head ($h_{v2}$): $$h_{v2} = \frac{V_2^2}{2g} = \frac{(1.0)^2}{2 \times 9.81} = \frac{1.0}{19.62} = \mathbf{0.051\text{ m}}$$
    • Water Surface Level ($\text{FSL}_2$): $$\text{FSL}_2 = \text{TEL}_2 - h_{v2} = 152.77 - 0.051 = \mathbf{152.719\text{ m}}$$
    • Bed Level at Exit = $\text{FSL}_2 - y_2 = 152.719 - 2.10 = \mathbf{150.619\text{ m}}$
2. Length of Contraction Transition ($L_c$):
  • Using standard contraction splay $2\text{H}:1\text{V}$ (splay angle $\theta \approx 26.5^\circ$): $$L_c = 2 \times \frac{B_1 - B_2}{2} = B_1 - B_2 = 18.0 - 6.3 = 11.7\text{ m}$$

3. Hind's Method Reversed Parabolic Water Surface Profile:
  • In Hind's method, the water surface is transitioned via two reversed parabolas meeting tangentially at mid-transition ($x = L_c / 2 = 6.0\text{ m}$).
  • Total rise in water surface: $\Delta y = \text{FSL}_2 - \text{FSL}_1 = 152.719 - 152.501 = +0.218\text{ m}$.
  • Divide transition into 4 equal intervals of $3.0\text{ m}$ each ($x = 0, 3, 6, 9, 12\text{ m}$):
    • At $x = 0\text{ m}$ (Entry): Bed width $B = 18.00\text{ m}$, side slope $1.5:1$, depth $y = 3.00\text{ m}$, Bed RL = $149.50\text{ m}$.
    • At $x = 3\text{ m}$: Bed width $B = 14.50\text{ m}$, side slope $1.125:1$, depth $y = 2.78\text{ m}$, Bed RL = $149.78\text{ m}$.
    • At $x = 6\text{ m}$ (Mid-point): Bed width $B = 11.00\text{ m}$, side slope $0.75:1$, depth $y = 2.55\text{ m}$, Bed RL = $150.06\text{ m}$.
    • At $x = 9\text{ m}$: Bed width $B = 8.25\text{ m}$, side slope $0.375:1$, depth $y = 2.32\text{ m}$, Bed RL = $150.34\text{ m}$.
    • At $x = 12\text{ m}$ (Exit / Flumed Throat): Bed width $B = 6.30\text{ m}$, side slope Vertical ($0:1$), depth $y = 2.10\text{ m}$, Bed RL = $150.62\text{ m}$.

topic: Straight Glacis Non-Metered Canal Fall Design
question:
Selection of fall location and design of an Unflumed Straight Glacis Fall:

**Tasks:**
1. Criteria for selecting the location of canal falls along a channel alignment.
2. Design the Crest and Cistern for an unflumed straight glacis non-metered fall.
solution:
1. Selection of Fall Location in a Canal:
  • Topographic Alignment: Located where ground slope significantly outpaces the permissible regime canal bed slope, balancing earthwork in cutting and filling.
  • Combined Structures: Preferred at sites where the fall can be combined with a bridge, road crossing, or canal head regulator to reduce overall construction cost.
  • Command Area Protection: Placed downstream of parent canal offtakes so full supply head for irrigation command is preserved.
2. Crest Design for $Q = 40\text{ m}^3/\text{s}$:
  • Discharge ($Q$) = $40\text{ m}^3/\text{s}$; Drop ($H_L$) = $1.60\text{ m}$; Bed width ($B$) = $26.0\text{ m}$
  • Since unflumed, crest length $L = B = 26.0\text{ m}$
  • Discharge intensity: $$q = \frac{40}{26} = 1.538\text{ m}^3/\text{s/m}$$
  • Head over crest ($H$) for broad-crested weir ($Q = 1.705 L H^{3/2}$): $$H = \left(\frac{q}{1.705}\right)^{2/3} = \left(\frac{1.538}{1.705}\right)^{2/3} = (0.902)^{2/3} = \mathbf{0.934\text{ m} \approx 0.93\text{ m}}$$
  • Crest Level = $\text{U/S FSL} - H = 101.00 - 0.93 = \mathbf{100.07\text{ m}}$
  • Height of crest above u/s bed ($h_c$) = $100.07 - 99.80 = 0.27\text{ m}$
  • Crest Width ($B_c$): $$B_c = \frac{2}{3}(H + h_c) = \frac{2}{3}(0.93 + 0.27) = \frac{2}{3}(1.20) = \mathbf{0.80\text{ m}}$$
  • Downstream Glacis: Provide $2.5\text{H}:1\text{V}$ straight slope.
3. Cistern Sizing & Hydraulic Jump:
  • Total energy line at jump foot: $$E_0 = H_L + H = 1.60 + 0.93 = 2.53\text{ m}$$
  • Pre-jump velocity and depth: $$V_1 \approx \sqrt{2g(E_0 - 0.5 y_1)} \approx \sqrt{2 \times 9.81 \times (2.53 - 0.15)} = \sqrt{46.7} = 6.83\text{ m/s}$$ $$y_1 = \frac{q}{V_1} = \frac{1.538}{6.83} = \mathbf{0.225\text{ m}}$$
  • Froude Number ($Fr_1$): $$Fr_1 = \frac{V_1}{\sqrt{g y_1}} = \frac{6.83}{\sqrt{9.81 \times 0.225}} = \frac{6.83}{1.486} = 4.60$$
  • Sequent depth ($y_2$): $$y_2 = \frac{0.225}{2}\left(\sqrt{1 + 8(4.60)^2} - 1\right) = 0.1125 \times (\sqrt{170.2} - 1) = 0.1125 \times 12.05 = \mathbf{1.36\text{ m}}$$
  • Length of Cistern ($L_c$): $$L_c = 5(y_2 - y_1) = 5(1.36 - 0.225) = 5 \times 1.135 = \mathbf{5.68\text{ m} \approx 6.0\text{ m}}$$
  • Cistern Bed Level: Depress by $0.25\text{ m}$ below d/s bed: $$\text{Cistern Bed Level} = 98.20 - 0.25 = \mathbf{97.95\text{ m}}$$

topic: Sarda Type Canal Fall Components & L-Section
question:
Selection of fall location and longitudinal section of Sarda Fall:

**Tasks:**
1. Selection criteria for locating falls in a canal network (balancing excavation, command area).
2. Draw a neat longitudinal section of a Sarda Type Fall labeling all components:
   - Crest wall, impervious floor, cistern, cutoffs, and energy dissipation blocks.
solution:
1. Selection of Fall Location in a Canal:
  • Earthwork Optimization: Positioned where ground slope outpaces the canal gradient to balance cut and fill volumes.
  • Combined Road Bridges: Co-locating falls with road bridges or cross-drainage structures saves abutment and wing wall costs.
  • Preservation of Full Command: Kept downstream of head regulators feeding minor channels to maintain required driving head.
2. Primary Structural Components of a Sarda Type Fall:
  • 1. Upstream Approach & Bed Protection: Upstream horizontal brick/concrete floor terminating in a vertical upstream cutoff curtain.
  • 2. Crest Wall:
    • Rectangular crest (for drops $H_L \le 0.9\text{ m}$) or Trapezoidal crest (for drops $H_L > 0.9\text{ m}$) with vertical upstream face and $1:8$ downstream slope.
    • Crest length equals channel bed width ($L = B$).
  • 3. Depressed Cistern: A sunken water cushion floor below downstream bed level to absorb the impact of the falling nappe and prevent floor erosion. Length $L_c = 5 \sqrt{H_L \cdot y}$, depression $x = \frac{1}{4}(H_L \cdot y)^{2/3}$.
  • 4. Downstream Impervious Floor: Extended impervious floor providing required Bligh/Khosla creep length.
  • 5. Downstream Cutoff Curtain & Launching Apron: Vertical cutoff wall preventing piping, flanked by flexible stone pitching.
  • 6. Deflector Sill: Small sill ($10\text{--}15\text{ cm}$ high) placed at the downstream end of the cistern to create a favorable ground roller.

topic: Stilling Basin Hydraulic Design
question:
Design a Stilling Basin for an Ogee Spillway:

**Determine & Design:**
1. Basin length ($L_b$) and basin floor depression depth.
2. Sizing and layout of chute blocks, baffle piers, and dentated end sill.

**Given Spillway Data:**
- Design Discharge Intensity: $q = 20\text{ m}^3/\text{s/m}$
- Spillway Crest Head: $H_d = 8.00\text{ m}$ | Drop from crest to river bed = $30.00\text{ m}$
solution:
1. Hydraulic Parameters:
  • Design discharge ($Q$) = $13875\text{ m}^3/\text{s}$; Crest length ($L$) = $183.0\text{ m}$
  • Discharge intensity ($q$) = $\frac{13875}{183} = \mathbf{75.82\text{ m}^3/\text{s/m}}$
  • Tailwater Level ($TWL$) = $180.30\text{ m}$; Tailwater depth ($y_{tw}$) = $13.80\text{ m}$
  • River Bed Level = $TWL - y_{tw} = 180.30 - 13.80 = \mathbf{166.50\text{ m}}$
  • Post-jump sequent depth ($y_2$) = $18.79\text{ m}$
2. Basin Floor Elevation & Depression Depth:
  • Required water level for hydraulic jump: $$\text{Required jump water level} = \text{Basin floor level} + y_2$$
  • To stabilize the jump within the basin, the tailwater level must match the post-jump depth: $$\text{Basin Floor Level} = TWL - y_2 = 180.30 - 18.79 = \mathbf{161.51\text{ m}}$$
  • Depth of Basin Depression below River Bed: $$\text{Basin Depth} = \text{River Bed Level} - \text{Basin Floor Level} = 166.50 - 161.51 = \mathbf{4.99\text{ m} \approx 5.00\text{ m}}$$
3. Basin Length ($L_b$):
  • Pre-jump depth ($y_1$) estimation from momentum relation: $$y_1 y_2 (y_1 + y_2) = \frac{2 q^2}{g} \implies y_1 (18.79)(18.79) \approx \frac{2(75.82)^2}{9.81} = \frac{11497}{9.81} = 1172$$ $$y_1 = \frac{1172}{(18.79)^2} = \frac{1172}{353.06} \approx \mathbf{3.32\text{ m}}$$
  • Incoming Froude Number: $$Fr_1 = \frac{q/y_1}{\sqrt{g y_1}} = \frac{75.82 / 3.32}{\sqrt{9.81 \times 3.32}} = \frac{22.84}{5.707} = \mathbf{4.00}$$
  • Using IS: 4997 Type-II stilling basin length: $$L_b = 4.3 \cdot y_2 = 4.3 \times 18.79 = \mathbf{80.80\text{ m} \approx 81.0\text{ m}}$$ $$(\text{Or by conservative rule: } L_b = 5 (y_2 - y_1) = 5(18.79 - 3.32) = 5 \times 15.47 = \mathbf{77.35\text{ m}})$$
  • Adopt Basin Length $L_b = \mathbf{80.0\text{ m}}$.
4. Sizing of Basin Blocks & Appurtenances (IS: 4997):
  • Chute Blocks:
    • Height ($h_1$) = $y_1 \approx 3.30\text{ m}$
    • Width and spacing = $y_1 \approx 3.30\text{ m}$
  • Baffle Piers / Basin Blocks:
    • For high velocity $> 15\text{ m/s}$ (IS Type-II), baffle blocks are omitted or replaced by heavy dentated sills to avoid cavitation damage.
    • Dentated end sill height ($h_3$) = $0.20 y_2 = 0.20 \times 18.79 = \mathbf{3.76\text{ m} \approx 3.80\text{ m}}$.
    • Dentated sill tooth width and spacing = $0.15 y_2 = 0.15 \times 18.79 = \mathbf{2.82\text{ m}}$.

question:

topic: Upper Nappe Profile & Side Wall Height Design
question:
Design of Upper Nappe Water Profile and Side Training Walls:

**Design Tasks:**
1. Upper nappe trajectory profile coordinates over an ogee crest.
2. Design height and freeboard for downstream side training walls.
solution:
1. Upper Nappe Profile Formulation (USBR / WES):
  • The upper surface of the sheet of water spilling over an aerated sharp-crested weir forms the upper nappe.
  • For design head $H_d$, coordinates of upper nappe ($x$ measured positive downstream from crest, $y$ vertical upward): $$y_u = H_d \left[1 - 0.5 \left(\frac{x}{H_d}\right)^{1.85}\right] \quad (\text{for downstream reach})$$
  • At the spillway crest ($x = 0$): Upper nappe height above crest is $H_d$.
  • Upstream of crest ($-x$ direction): The upper nappe rises slightly due to backwater stagnation before leveling off to the reservoir water surface ($H_d + h_v$).
2. Height of Training / Side Wall Design:
  • Training walls flanking the spillway chute must contain high-velocity discharge and spray without overtopping.
  • Water Depth on Chute ($d$): At any section along the chute with velocity $V$, clear water depth $d = \frac{q}{V}$.
  • Air Entrainment Allowance: High-velocity flow entrains air, swelling the flow thickness. Bulking factor: $$d_{bulked} = \frac{d}{1 - C_{air}} \approx 1.20\text{ to }1.25\, d$$
  • Freeboard ($FB$): Freeboard above bulked water surface based on flow velocity: $$FB = 0.60 + 0.04 V \cdot d^{1/3}$$
  • Total Height of Side Wall ($H_{wall}$): $$H_{wall} = d_{bulked} + FB = 1.25 d + (0.60 + 0.04 V d^{1/3})$$

topic: Gravity Dam Stability under Earthquake & Extreme Uplift
question:
Stress analysis of a Gravity dam under **Reservoir Full with Earthquake and Extreme Uplift condition**:

**Calculate:**
1. Principal stress ($\sigma_1$) developed at the heel and toe.
2. Shear stress ($\tau_0$) developed at the heel and toe of the dam profile.

**Given Seismic Coefficients (uniform over depth):**
- Horizontal acceleration coefficient: $\alpha_h = 0.10$
- Vertical acceleration coefficient: $\alpha_v = 0.08$
solution:
1. Additional Dynamic & Extreme Uplift Forces on Figure-1 Profile:
  • Seismic Coefficients & Inertia Forces:
    • Given coefficients: $\alpha_h = 0.10$ (horizontal D/S), $\alpha_v = 0.08$ (vertical downward reduction)

topic: Elementary Profile of Gravity Dam Derivation
question:
Elementary Profile of a Gravity Dam:

**Derivations & Concepts:**
1. What is the theoretical elementary profile of a gravity dam?
2. Derive the expressions for determining base width ($B$) based on the stress criterion (no tension at heel).
solution:
1. Concept of Elementary Profile:
  • The elementary profile of a gravity dam is a theoretical right-angled triangular cross-section having zero top width at full reservoir level, a vertical upstream face, and a sloping downstream face.
2. Derivation of Base Width based on Stress Criterion (No Tension):
  • For concrete/masonry, tensile strength is negligible. To avoid tension at the upstream heel when the reservoir is full, the resultant force $R$ must pass through the downstream middle third point (eccentricity $e \le B/6$).
  • Taking moment equilibrium about the toe (resultant at distance $\bar{x} = B/3$ from toe): $$W = \frac{1}{2} B H \gamma_c = \frac{1}{2} B H S_c \gamma_w$$ $$P = \frac{1}{2} \gamma_w H^2 \quad (\text{acting at } H/3 \text{ above base})$$ $$U = \frac{1}{2} c \gamma_w H B \quad (\text{acting at } 2B/3 \text{ from toe, where } c = \text{uplift factor})$$
  • Equating restoring moment to overturning moment about the resultant point ($B/3$ from toe): $$(W - U)\left(\frac{B}{3}\right) = P\left(\frac{H}{3}\right)$$ $$\left[\frac{1}{2} B H \gamma_w (S_c - c)\right] \left(\frac{B}{3}\right) = \left[\frac{1}{2} \gamma_w H^2\right] \left(\frac{H}{3}\right)$$ $$B^2 (S_c - c) = H^2$$ $$\mathbf{B = \frac{H}{\sqrt{S_c - c}}}$$
  • When uplift pressure is fully relieved or neglected ($c = 0$): $$\mathbf{B = \frac{H}{\sqrt{S_c}}}$$
  • For typical concrete with $S_c = 2.4$ and $c = 1.0$: $$B = \frac{H}{\sqrt{2.4 - 1.0}} = \frac{H}{\sqrt{1.4}} \approx \mathbf{0.845 H}$$

topic: Hydraulic Jump on Sloping Glacis Water Surface Profile
question:
Stepwise procedure for plotting the location of a hydraulic jump on a sloping glacis:

**Stepwise Procedure:**
1. Formulate energy and momentum equations for pre-jump and post-jump flow.
2. Plot tailwater rating curve and jump rating curve to find intersection location.
solution:
1. Stepwise Procedure for Plotting Hydraulic Jump Location on Sloping Glacis:
  • Step 1: Compute Upstream Specific Energy: Calculate the Total Energy Line (TEL) upstream of the weir crest: $\text{TEL} = \text{Crest RL} + H_e$.
  • Step 2: Plot Pre-Jump Supercritical Profile ($y_1$):
    • At selected bed levels $Z$ down the sloping glacis, compute available specific energy $E = \text{TEL} - Z$.
    • Solve specific energy relation $E = y_1 + \frac{q^2}{2g y_1^2}$ for pre-jump depth $y_1$.
    • Water surface elevation before jump $= Z + y_1$.
  • Step 3: Plot Post-Jump Sequent Depth Profile ($J_2C$):
    • For each computed $y_1$ and Froude number $Fr_1 = \frac{q/y_1}{\sqrt{g y_1}}$, calculate conjugate post-jump depth $y_2$: $$y_2 = \frac{y_1}{2}\left(\sqrt{1 + 8 Fr_1^2} - 1\right)$$
    • Post-jump water level elevation $= Z + y_2$. Plot this as the Jump Rating Curve ($J_2C$) along the glacis.
  • Step 4: Superimpose Tailwater Rating Curve (TWC): Plot the actual downstream tailwater level on the same elevation profile.
  • Step 5: Identify Jump Location: The point where the $J_2C$ profile intersects the TWC line marks the exact toe position of the hydraulic jump on the sloping glacis.

topic: Earth Dam Failures & Safety Measures
question:
Causes of Failure of Earth Dams:

**Discuss in Brief:**
1. Hydraulic failures (overtopping, wave erosion, gullying).
2. Seepage failures (piping, sloughing, foundation boil).
3. Structural failures (slope failure, foundation shear failure, earthquake damage).
solution:
1. Hydraulic Failures:
  • Overtopping: Occurs when flood discharge exceeds spillway capacity, causing water to wash over and breach the crest.
  • Wave Erosion: Surface wind waves carve notches into unprotected upstream slopes.
  • Toe & Gully Erosion: Tailwater cross-currents or concentrated rain runoff cut grooves along embankment edges.
2. Seepage Failures:
  • Piping through Dam Body: Progressive internal washing of fine particles forms continuous tubular cavities along the phreatic line.
  • Piping through Foundation: Uncontrolled seepage through permeable gravel/sand strata erodes foundation support.
  • Sloughing of Downstream Toe: Complete saturation of the toe reduces effective soil shear strength, causing progressive progressive unraveling.
3. Structural Failures:
  • Upstream Slope Slide during Sudden Drawdown: High pore pressures trapped inside the upstream shell trigger deep circular rotational shear slides.
  • Downstream Slope Slide during Steady Seepage: High phreatic line under full reservoir saturates the downstream shell, causing slope instability.
  • Foundation Shear Failure & Liquefaction: Soft clay foundation seams yield, or seismic shaking induces liquefaction in loose saturated sand layers.

topic: Earthen Dam Phreatic Line (Casagrande's Method) & Seepage
question:
Determine the Phreatic Line for an Earthen Dam using Casagrande's Method:

**Calculate & Plot:**
1. Plot the Phreatic Line using Casagrande's focal method.
2. Compute seepage discharge per unit length of the dam ($q$).

**Given Dam Geometry & Soil Data:**
- Dam Height: $20\text{ m}$ | Freeboard: $2\text{ m}$
- Top Width: $6\text{ m}$ | Bottom Width: $146\text{ m}$
- Upstream Slope: $4\text{H} : 1\text{V}$ | Downstream Slope: $3\text{H} : 1\text{V}$
- Length of Horizontal Toe Filter: $30\text{ m}$
- Soil Permeability: $k = 6 \times 10^{-4}\text{ cm/s}$
solution:
1. Geometric Parameters:
  • Dam Height ($H$) = $20.0\text{ m}$; Freeboard ($FB$) = $2.0\text{ m}$
  • Water depth upstream ($h$) = $20 - 2 = 18.0\text{ m}$
  • Top width ($b$) = $6.0\text{ m}$; Bottom width ($B$) = $146.0\text{ m}$
  • U/S slope = $4\text{H}:1\text{V}$; D/S slope = $3\text{H}:1\text{V}$
  • Horizontal filter length from downstream toe ($L_f$) = $30.0\text{ m}$
  • Permeability ($k$) = $6 \times 10^{-4}\text{ cm/s} = 6 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m/s}$
2. Focus Location & Distance ($d$):
  • Focus $F$ is at the upstream inner tip of the horizontal toe filter.
  • Distance of focus $F$ from upstream heel: $$\text{Dist}_{heel\to F} = B - L_f = 146.0 - 30.0 = \mathbf{116.0\text{ m}}$$
  • Water entry point $A$ on upstream face: horizontal distance from heel $= 4 \times 18 = 72.0\text{ m}$.
  • Casagrande entry shift $\Delta = 72.0\text{ m} \implies 0.3 \Delta = 21.6\text{ m}$.
  • Distance of starting point $A_0$ from heel $= 72.0 - 21.6 = 50.4\text{ m}$.
  • Horizontal distance $d$ from starting point $A_0$ to focus $F$: $$d = 116.0 - 50.4 = \mathbf{65.60\text{ m}}$$
3. Basic Parabola Equation:
  • Focal parameter ($y_0$): $$y_0 = \sqrt{d^2 + h^2} - d = \sqrt{(65.60)^2 + (18.0)^2} - 65.60 = \sqrt{4303.36 + 324} - 65.60 = \sqrt{4627.36} - 65.60 = 68.025 - 65.60 = \mathbf{2.425\text{ m}}$$
  • Equation of the base parabola with origin at focus $F$: $$x = \frac{y^2 - y_0^2}{2y_0} = \frac{y^2 - (2.425)^2}{2(2.425)} = \mathbf{\frac{y^2 - 5.88}{4.85}}$$
4. Phreatic Line Coordinates & Seepage Discharge:
  • At $y = 0\text{ m}$ (filter tip): $x = -y_0/2 = -1.21\text{ m}$
  • At $y = 6\text{ m}$: $x = \frac{36 - 5.88}{4.85} = 6.21\text{ m}$
  • At $y = 12\text{ m}$: $x = \frac{144 - 5.88}{4.85} = 28.48\text{ m}$
  • At $y = 18\text{ m}$ ($A_0$): $x = \frac{324 - 5.88}{4.85} = 65.59\text{ m} \approx 65.60\text{ m}$
  • Seepage Discharge per Unit Length ($q$): $$q = k \cdot y_0 = (6 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m/s}) \times 2.425\text{ m} = \mathbf{1.455 \times 10^{-5}\text{ m}^3/\text{s per meter length}}$$
  • In practical units: $q = 0.01455\text{ L/s/m} \approx 52.38\text{ Liters/hour per meter length}$.

topic: Siphon Spillway Operating Principle & Discharge Derivation
question:
Functioning and discharge derivation of a Saddle Siphon Spillway:

**Tasks:**
1. Explain the working principle of a saddle siphon spillway with a neat sketch.
2. Derive the expression for Discharge ($Q$) passing through the siphon unit in terms of throat dimensions.
solution:
1. Functioning of a Saddle Siphon Spillway:
  • A saddle siphon spillway is a closed reinforced concrete conduit built in the form of an inverted U-shaped saddle over a dam crest.
  • Phase 1: Weir Flow: When the reservoir rises slightly above the crest, a small trickle of water flows over the crown like a broad-crested weir.
  • Phase 2: Priming: As overflow strikes a deflector lip or lower sealing basin, it forms an airtight water curtain, entraining and expelling trapped air. The resulting pressure drop inside the conduit primes the siphon into full pipe flow under negative atmospheric pressure.
  • Phase 3: Siphonic Flow: Water discharges at high velocity under the full operating head ($H$) between the reservoir surface and tailwater/outlet.
  • Phase 4: Depriming: When the reservoir drops back to FRL, the air vent emerges above the water surface, admitting atmospheric air to break the siphonic vacuum and stop flow.
2. Derivation of Siphon Discharge Formula:
  • Applying Bernoulli's Theorem between point $1$ in the reservoir and point $2$ at the siphon throat (throat width $b$, height $h$, total throat area $A = b \cdot h$): $$\frac{P_1}{\gamma_w} + \frac{V_1^2}{2g} + Z_1 = \frac{P_2}{\gamma_w} + \frac{V_2^2}{2g} + Z_2 + h_L$$
  • For a free-discharging siphon with total operating head $H$ between reservoir surface and outlet center: $$V = C_v \sqrt{2g H}$$
  • Accounting for flow contraction and losses via overall coefficient of discharge $C_d$: $$Q = C_d \cdot A \cdot \sqrt{2g H}$$ $$\mathbf{Q = C_d \cdot (b \cdot h) \cdot \sqrt{2g H}}$$
  • When throat curvature is sharp, velocity distribution follows a free vortex ($v \cdot r = C$). Siphon discharge in terms of inner radius ($R_1$) and outer radius ($R_2$): $$Q = C_d \cdot b \cdot \sqrt{2g H} \cdot \frac{h}{\ln(R_2 / R_1)}$$

topic: Energy Dissipating Devices Classification
question:
Differentiate between Hydraulic Jump Type and Bucket Type Energy Dissipaters:

**Comparison Points:**
1. Hydraulic mechanism (standing wave dissipation vs. roller / trajectory jet).
2. Sub-classes (USBR Stilling Basins I-IV vs. solid/slotted roller buckets and ski-jump buckets).
3. Recommended site, tailwater, and rock foundation conditions for each type.
solution:
1. Contrast between Hydraulic Jump & Bucket Type Dissipaters:
  • Dissipation Mechanism:
    • Hydraulic Jump Type: Converts kinetic energy into thermal energy and macro-turbulent eddies within a standing hydraulic jump contained on a paved horizontal or sloping concrete apron.
    • Bucket Type: Deflects the high-velocity jet into an upward air trajectory (ski-jump) or creates interacting submerged rollers (roller bucket) to dissipate energy away from the structure.
  • Structure Size & Economics:
    • Hydraulic Jump Type: Requires a long, heavy concrete apron ($5\text{ to }6$ times sequent depth $y_2$) with massive side training walls; more expensive for high dams.
    • Bucket Type: Requires only a short curved circular bucket lip; highly economical for high dams.
2. Sub-Classes:
  • Hydraulic Jump Sub-classes (IS: 4997): Type I (plain horizontal apron), Type II (chute blocks + dentated sill), Type III (chute blocks + small baffle piers + solid sill), Type IV (wave suppressor apron).
  • Bucket Type Sub-classes: Ski-Jump (Flip) Bucket, Solid Roller Bucket, Slotted Roller Bucket.
3. Recommended Situations:
  • Hydraulic Jump Stilling Basin: Recommended for low to medium head spillways ($H < 30\text{ m}$) where the tailwater rating curve (TWC) closely matches the jump rating curve ($J_2C$), and where the downstream river bed consists of erodible alluvium or fractured rock.
  • Ski-Jump Bucket: Recommended for medium to high dams ($H > 30\text{ m}$) founded on massive, sound bedrock with low tailwater depth ($y_{tw} \ll y_2$).
  • Roller Bucket: Recommended for high dams where tailwater is excessively deep ($y_{tw} > 1.2 y_2$).

  • Given Tailwater depth: $y_{tw} = 1.1 \cdot D_2$ (where $D_2$ is the theoretical sequent depth $y_2$).
2. Conjugate Depths ($D_1$ and $D_2$):
  • Energy loss formula for a classical hydraulic jump: $$\Delta H_L = \frac{(D_2 - D_1)^3}{4 D_1 D_2} = 1.40\text{ m}$$
  • Momentum relation for rectangular channel: $$D_1 D_2 (D_1 + D_2) = \frac{2 q^2}{g} = \frac{2 \times (14.0)^2}{9.81} = \frac{392}{9.81} = \mathbf{39.96\text{ m}^3}$$
  • Solving simultaneously by trial:
    • Try $D_1 = 1.0\text{ m}$: $D_2(1 + D_2) = 39.96 \implies D_2 \approx 5.85\text{ m}$.
      Check loss: $\Delta H_L = \frac{(5.85 - 1.0)^3}{4 \times 1.0 \times 5.85} = \frac{(4.85)^3}{23.4} = \frac{114.1}{23.4} = 4.87\text{ m} > 1.40\text{ m}$.
    • Try $D_1 = 1.45\text{ m}$: $D_2(1.45 + D_2) = \frac{39.96}{1.45} = 27.56 \implies D_2 \approx 4.58\text{ m}$.
      Check loss: $\Delta H_L = \frac{(4.58 - 1.45)^3}{4 \times 1.45 \times 4.58} = \frac{(3.13)^3}{26.56} = \frac{30.66}{26.56} = 1.15\text{ m}$.
    • Exact solution: $\mathbf{D_1 = 1.38\text{ m}}$ and $\mathbf{D_2 = 4.75\text{ m}}$.
      Check loss: $\Delta H_L = \frac{(4.75 - 1.38)^3}{4 \times 1.38 \times 4.75} = \frac{(3.37)^3}{26.22} = \frac{38.27}{26.22} = \mathbf{1.46\text{ m} \approx 1.40\text{ m}}$.
  • Incoming Froude Number ($Fr_1$): $$Fr_1 = \frac{q / D_1}{\sqrt{g D_1}} = \frac{14.0 / 1.38}{\sqrt{9.81 \times 1.38}} = \frac{10.14}{3.68} = \mathbf{2.76}$$
3. Basin Floor Elevation & Dimensions:
  • Tailwater depth ($y_{tw}$) = $1.1 \times D_2 = 1.1 \times 4.75 = \mathbf{5.23\text{ m}}$
  • Downstream Tailwater Level = $\text{D/S TEL} - \frac{V_2^2}{2g} = 302.20 - \frac{(14 / 5.23)^2}{2 \times 9.81} = 302.20 - 0.36 = \mathbf{301.84\text{ m}}$
  • Basin Floor Elevation: $$\text{Floor RL} = \text{Tailwater Level} - y_{tw} = 301.84 - 5.23 = \mathbf{296.61\text{ m}}$$
  • Length of Stilling Basin ($L_b$):
    • For $Fr_1 = 2.76$ (oscillating jump range), provide IS: 4997 Type-I horizontal apron: $$L_b = 5 \times D_2 = 5 \times 4.75 = \mathbf{23.75\text{ m} \approx 24.0\text{ m}}$$
  • End Sill: Provide solid triangular end sill of height $h_3 = 0.10 D_2 = 0.10 \times 4.75 = \mathbf{0.48\text{ m} \approx 0.50\text{ m}}$ with upstream slope $2\text{H}:1\text{V}$.

topic: Barrage & Weir Gate Discharge Calculation
question:
A weir has $52$ vertical gates of span $10\text{ m}$ each:

**Calculate:**
1. Maximum flood discharge ($Q$) that can safely pass over the weir without exceeding FRL.

**Given Weir Data:**
- Number of Gates = $52$ | Span of each Gate = $10.00\text{ m}$
- Full Reservoir Level (FRL) = $110.00\text{ m}$
- End Contraction Coefficients: Piers $K_p = 0.02$, Abutments $K_a = 0.10$
- Coefficient of Discharge: $C_d = 1.70$ (Neglect velocity of approach)
solution:
1. Geometric & Flow Parameters:
  • Number of vertical gates ($n$) = $52$; Clear span of each gate ($L$) = $10.0\text{ m}$
  • Total clear crest length ($L_{clear}$) = $52 \times 10.0 = 520.0\text{ m}$
  • Number of intermediate piers ($N$) = $n - 1 = 51$
  • Pier contraction coefficient ($K_p$) = $0.02$; Abutment contraction coefficient ($K_a$) = $0.10$
  • Discharge coefficient ($C_d$) = $1.70$; Full Reservoir Level ($FRL$) = $110.0\text{ m}$
  • Assume standard weir crest level at sill $= 106.0\text{ m}$ (so operating head $H = 110.0 - 106.0 = 4.0\text{ m}$); or if crest is at FRL, gates open fully under depth $H$. Let design head over crest $= H = 4.0\text{ m}$.
2. Effective Crest Length ($L_e$):
  • Using Francis formula for end contractions: $$L_e = L_{clear} - 2(N K_p + K_a) H$$ $$2(N K_p + K_a) = 2(51 \times 0.02 + 0.10) = 2(1.02 + 0.10) = 2(1.12) = \mathbf{2.24}$$ $$L_e = 520.0 - 2.24 H$$
  • For design head $H = 4.0\text{ m}$: $$L_e = 520.0 - (2.24 \times 4.0) = 520.0 - 8.96 = \mathbf{511.04\text{ m}}$$
3. Maximum Flood Discharge Calculation:
  • Weir discharge formula (neglecting velocity of approach): $$Q = C_d \cdot L_e \cdot H^{3/2}$$ $$Q = 1.70 \times 511.04 \times (4.0)^{3/2} = 1.70 \times 511.04 \times 8.0 = 1.70 \times 4088.3 = \mathbf{6950.1\text{ m}^3/\text{s (cumecs)}}$$
  • Parametric expression for any operating head $H$: $$Q = 1.70 \times (520.0 - 2.24 H) \times H^{3/2} = \mathbf{884 H^{3/2} - 3.808 H^{5/2}\text{ cumecs}}$$

topic: Barrage Waterways & Crest Levels Design
question:
Fix crest levels and waterways for Barrage and undersluices portion at a diversion headwork:

**Determine & Design:**
1. Crest levels and clear waterways for Barrage and Undersluice bays.
2. Upstream and downstream floor cutoffs using Lacey's regime theory.

**Given River Data:**
- High Flood Discharge: $Q = 10{,}000\text{ m}^3/\text{s}$ (cumecs)
- Average River Bed Level = $299.50\text{ m}$ | HFL before construction = $305.00\text{ m}$
- Permissible Afflux = $1.00\text{ m}$ | Pond Level = $303.00\text{ m}$
- Lacey's Silt Factor: $f = 1.0$
solution:
1. Hydraulic Parameters & Waterways:
  • High Flood Discharge ($Q$) = $10000\text{ m}^3/\text{s}$; River bed level = $299.50\text{ m}$
  • HFL before construction = $305.00\text{ m}$; Afflux = $1.00\text{ m} \implies \text{Affluxed HFL} = 305.00 + 1.00 = \mathbf{306.00\text{ m}}$
  • Pond Level ($PL$) = $303.00\text{ m}$; Lacey's silt factor ($f$) = $1.0$
  • Regime waterway by Lacey: $$P = 4.75 \sqrt{Q} = 4.75 \sqrt{10000} = 4.75 \times 100 = \mathbf{475.0\text{ m}}$$
2. Undersluice Sizing & Crest Level:
  • Undersluice capacity provided for $20\%$ of flood discharge = $2000\text{ m}^3/\text{s}$.
  • Undersluice Crest Level: Kept at average river bed level to maintain deep silt pocket: $$\text{Undersluice Crest Level} = \mathbf{299.50\text{ m}}$$
  • Undersluice Waterway: Provide $8$ bays of $10\text{ m}$ each with $2\text{ m}$ piers: $$\text{Clear Undersluice Waterway} = 8 \times 10.0 = \mathbf{80.0\text{ m}}$$
3. Barrage Bay Sizing & Crest Level:
  • Remaining clear waterway for main barrage = $475 - 80 = 395\text{ m}$.
  • Provide $40$ bays of $10\text{ m}$ each $\implies$ Clear barrage waterway = $\mathbf{400.0\text{ m}}$.
  • Barrage Bay Crest Level: Kept $1.20\text{ m}$ above undersluice crest level: $$\text{Barrage Crest Level} = 299.50 + 1.20 = \mathbf{300.70\text{ m}}$$
  • Discharge capacity check at affluxed HFL ($306.00\text{ m}$):
    • Head on barrage crest $H_1 = 306.00 - 300.70 = 5.30\text{ m} \implies Q_1 = 1.7 \times 400 \times (5.30)^{1.5} = 8289\text{ m}^3/\text{s}$
    • Head on undersluice crest $H_2 = 306.00 - 299.50 = 6.50\text{ m} \implies Q_2 = 1.7 \times 80 \times (6.50)^{1.5} = 2253\text{ m}^3/\text{s}$
    • Total discharge capacity = $8289 + 2253 = \mathbf{10542\text{ m}^3/\text{s}} > 10000\text{ m}^3/\text{s} \quad (\mathbf{Safe})$
4. Summary:
  • Affluxed HFL = $306.00\text{ m}$; Pond Level = $303.00\text{ m}$
  • Undersluice: 8 bays of $10\text{ m}$, Crest Level = $299.50\text{ m}$
  • Barrage: 40 bays of $10\text{ m}$, Crest Level = $300.70\text{ m}$
  • Total Clear Waterway = $480\text{ m}$

topic: Vertical Drop Weir Design via Bligh's Creep Theory
question:
Design a Vertical Drop Weir and impervious floor:

**Determine & Design:**
1. Crest level and impervious floor length using Bligh's Creep Theory ($C = 12$).
2. Draw a neat cross-section sketch.

**Given Weir Data:**
- High Flood Discharge: $Q = 3{,}150\text{ m}^3/\text{s}$ (cumecs)
- HFL before construction = $193.00\text{ m}$ | River Bed Level = $186.00\text{ m}$
- Canal FSL = $191.00\text{ m}$ | Bligh's Creep Coefficient: $C = 12$
- Lacey's Silt Factor: $f = 1.0$
- Weir Wall Dimensions: Top Width = $3.00\text{ m}$, Bottom Width = $8.00\text{ m}$
solution:
1. Hydraulic Parameters & Waterway:
  • Discharge ($Q$) = $3150\text{ m}^3/\text{s}$; Bed level = $186.00\text{ m}$; Canal FSL = $191.00\text{ m}$
  • HFL before construction = $193.00\text{ m}$; Assume afflux = $1.00\text{ m} \implies \text{Affluxed HFL} = 194.00\text{ m}$
  • Lacey's regime crest length: $$L = 4.75 \sqrt{3150} = 4.75 \times 56.125 = \mathbf{267.0\text{ m}}$$
  • Pond Level: Provide $1.0\text{ m}$ driving head above canal FSL: $$\text{Pond Level} = 191.00 + 1.00 = \mathbf{192.00\text{ m}}$$
  • Weir Crest Level with $1.0\text{ m}$ falling shutters: $$\text{Crest Level} = 192.00 - 1.00 = \mathbf{191.00\text{ m}}$$
  • Weir wall geometry given: Top width = $3.0\text{ m}$, Base width = $8.0\text{ m}$
  • Maximum static seepage head ($H_{seep}$) = $\text{Pond Level} - \text{Bed Level} = 192.00 - 186.00 = \mathbf{6.00\text{ m}}$
2. Impervious Floor Length (Bligh's Creep Theory):
  • Total creep length required: $$L_{creep} = C \cdot H_{seep} = 12 \times 6.00 = \mathbf{72.00\text{ m}}$$
  • Cutoffs:
    • Upstream cutoff depth $d_1 = 3.0\text{ m} \implies \text{vertical creep} = 2 \times 3.0 = 6.0\text{ m}$
    • Downstream cutoff depth $d_2 = 4.0\text{ m} \implies \text{vertical creep} = 2 \times 4.0 = 8.0\text{ m}$
    • Total vertical creep = $6.0 + 8.0 = 14.0\text{ m}$
  • Total horizontal impervious floor length required: $$L_h = 72.00 - 14.00 = \mathbf{58.00\text{ m}}$$
  • Floor Layout:
    • Upstream horizontal floor length = $14.0\text{ m}$
    • Weir wall base width = $8.0\text{ m}$
    • Downstream horizontal floor length ($L_{ds}$) = $58.00 - 14.00 - 8.00 = \mathbf{36.00\text{ m}}$
3. Downstream Floor Thicknesses:
  • Concrete specific gravity $G = 2.24 \implies G - 1 = 1.24$
  • At downstream toe of weir ($28.0\text{ m}$ creep from upstream):
    Residual head $h_1 = 6.00 \times \left(1 - \frac{28.0}{72.0}\right) = 6.00 \times 0.611 = 3.67\text{ m}$ $$t_1 = \frac{4}{3} \frac{3.67}{1.24} = \mathbf{3.95\text{ m} \approx 4.00\text{ m}}$$
  • At mid-length of d/s floor ($18\text{ m}$ from toe):
    Residual head $h_2 = 6.00 \times \left(1 - \frac{46.0}{72.0}\right) = 6.00 \times 0.361 = 2.17\text{ m}$ $$t_2 = \frac{4}{3} \frac{2.17}{1.24} = \mathbf{2.33\text{ m} \approx 2.35\text{ m}}$$
  • At downstream end (before cutoff):
    Residual head $h_3 = 6.00 \times \left(1 - \frac{64.0}{72.0}\right) = 0.67\text{ m}$ $$t_3 = \frac{4}{3} \frac{0.67}{1.24} = \mathbf{0.72\text{ m} \to \text{Provide nominal minimum } 1.00\text{ m}}$$

topic: Canal Regulation Works: Head & Cross Regulators
question:
Canal Regulation Works:

**Discuss in Detail:**
1. Definition and classification of canal regulation works.
2. Necessity, hydraulic functions, and operational differences between Cross Regulators and Head Regulators.
solution:
1. Concept of Canal Regulation Works:
  • Canal regulation works are hydraulic control structures built across or at the offtake of irrigation canals to control water levels, regulate discharge distribution, prevent excessive silt entry, and safeguard channels during emergencies.
2. Necessity and Functions:
  • Canal Head Regulator (at the Offtake of Distributary):
    • Discharge Control: Regulates the volume of water admitted from the parent main canal into the offtaking channel according to crop demand.
    • Silt Exclusion: High crest elevation and breast walls ensure only silt-free surface water enters the offtaking canal.
    • Flow Measurement: Calibrated gate openings serve as a discharge measuring flume.
    • Canal Closure: Shuts off offtake supply during canal maintenance, breaches, or non-demand periods.
  • Cross Regulator (across the Parent Canal):
    • Water Level Heading: Raises the parent canal water level during low flow stages so offtaking canals can draw their full authorized supply.
    • Discharge Routing: Controls flow distribution among downstream branch canals.
    • Surplus Escape: Works in conjunction with canal escapes to divert surplus floodwater during heavy rains.
    • Inspection & Crossing: Often combined with road bridges to provide rural roadway access across the canal.

topic: Canal Fluming & Transitions: Mitra's & Chaturvedi's Methods
question:
Design a Channel Transition at a Cross Drainage Work using R. S. Chaturvedi and Mitra's methods:

**Tasks:**
1. Derive Mitra's hyperbolic transition formula ($B_x = \frac{B_1 B_2 L}{L B_1 - x(B_1 - B_2)}$).
2. Compute channel fluming transition coordinates using Chaturvedi's and Mitra's methods.

**Given Channel Dimensions:**
- Original Bed Width ($B_1$) = $15.00\text{ m}$
- Flumed Bed Width ($B_2$) = $10.00\text{ m}$
- Length of Flume ($L$) = $15.00\text{ m}$
solution:
1. Derivation of Mitra's Hyperbolic Transition Formula:
  • Consider a flumed channel transitioning from normal bed width $B_n$ to flumed throat width $B_f$ over length $L$.
  • Mitra assumed that the rate of change of specific energy per unit length is constant ($\frac{dE}{dx} = \text{constant}$). For negligible depth variation ($y \approx \text{const}$), the velocity changes at a uniform rate along the length: $$\frac{dV}{dx} = \text{constant} \implies V_x = V_n + \frac{x}{L}(V_f - V_n)$$
  • By continuity of discharge ($Q = B_x \cdot y \cdot V_x = \text{const}$), channel width is inversely proportional to velocity: $$\frac{1}{B_x} \propto V_x \implies \frac{1}{B_x} = \frac{1}{B_n} + \frac{x}{L}\left(\frac{1}{B_f} - \frac{1}{B_n}\right)$$
  • Simplifying algebraically: $$\frac{1}{B_x} = \frac{L B_f + x(B_n - B_f)}{B_n B_f L}$$ $$\mathbf{B_x = \frac{B_n \cdot B_f \cdot L}{L \cdot B_f + x(B_n - B_f)} = \frac{B_n \cdot B_f \cdot L}{L \cdot B_n - x'(B_n - B_f)}}$$
2. Application of Mitra's Method ($B_n = 15\text{ m}, B_f = 10\text{ m}, L = 15\text{ m}$):
  • With $x$ measured from the flumed section ($x = 0$ at flume, $x = 15\text{ m}$ at normal section): $$B_x = \frac{15 \times 10 \times 15}{15 \times 10 + x(15 - 10)} = \frac{2250}{150 + 5x} = \mathbf{\frac{450}{30 + x}}$$
  • Bed widths along length:
    • At $x = 0\text{ m}$ (Flume throat): $B_0 = \frac{450}{30} = \mathbf{10.00\text{ m}}$
    • At $x = 3\text{ m}$: $B_3 = \frac{450}{33} = \mathbf{13.64\text{ m}}$
    • At $x = 7.5\text{ m}$ (Mid-point): $B_{7.5} = \frac{450}{37.5} = \mathbf{12.00\text{ m}}$
    • At $x = 11.25\text{ m}$: $B_{11.25} = \frac{450}{41.25} = \mathbf{10.91\text{ m}}$
    • At $x = 15\text{ m}$ (Normal section): $B_{15} = \frac{450}{45} = \mathbf{15.00\text{ m}}$ (Expansion direction)
3. Application of R.S. Chaturvedi's Method:
  • Chaturvedi proposed a semi-cubical parabolic transition equation: $$B_x = B_f + (B_n - B_f) \left[1 - \left(1 - \frac{x}{L}\right)^{3/2}\right]$$
  • Substituting given values ($B_f = 10, B_n - B_f = 5, L = 15$): $$B_x = 10 + 5 \left[1 - \left(1 - \frac{x}{15}\right)^{3/2}\right]$$
  • Bed widths by Chaturvedi's method:
    • At $x = 0\text{ m}$: $B_0 = 10 + 5[1 - 1] = \mathbf{10.00\text{ m}}$
    • At $x = 3.75\text{ m}$ ($x/L = 0.25$): $B = 10 + 5[1 - (0.75)^{1.5}] = 10 + 5[1 - 0.650] = 10 + 1.75 = \mathbf{11.75\text{ m}}$
    • At $x = 7.5\text{ m}$ ($x/L = 0.50$): $B = 10 + 5[1 - (0.50)^{1.5}] = 10 + 5[1 - 0.354] = 10 + 3.23 = \mathbf{13.23\text{ m}}$
    • At $x = 11.25\text{ m}$ ($x/L = 0.75$): $B = 10 + 5[1 - (0.25)^{1.5}] = 10 + 5[1 - 0.125] = 10 + 4.38 = \mathbf{14.38\text{ m}}$
    • At $x = 15\text{ m}$ ($x/L = 1.0$): $B = 10 + 5[1 - 0] = \mathbf{15.00\text{ m}}$

topic: Sarda Type Canal Fall Design
question:
Design the Crest, Cistern, and impervious floor for a Canal Fall:

**Determine & Design:**
1. Selection justification for Sarda Type Fall.
2. Crest dimensions (length, top width, base width, crest level).
3. Cistern dimensions (length, depression depth, cistern bed level).
4. Total impervious floor length using Bligh's Creep Theory ($C = 8$).

**Given Canal Data:**
- Full Supply Discharge: $Q = 15\text{ m}^3/\text{s}$ (cumecs) | Drop: $H_L = 1.50\text{ m}$
- Full Supply Level (FSL): Upstream = $218.30\text{ m}$, Downstream = $216.80\text{ m}$
- Full Supply Depth (FSD): Upstream = $1.80\text{ m}$, Downstream = $1.80\text{ m}$
- Bed Width: Upstream = $26.00\text{ m}$, Downstream = $26.00\text{ m}$
- Bed Level: Upstream = $216.50\text{ m}$, Downstream = $215.00\text{ m}$
- Bligh's Creep Coefficient: $C = 8$
solution:
1. Selection of Type of Canal Fall:
  • Selected Type: Sarda Type Fall (with Trapezoidal Crest).
  • Reason for Selection:
    • The drop ($H_L = 1.50\text{ m}$) is moderate ($\le 1.5\text{ m}$) and discharge ($Q = 15\text{ m}^3/\text{s}$) is substantial.
    • Sarda falls are unflumed ($L = B$), requiring no expensive fluming contraction/expansion transitions.
    • Trapezoidal crest with vertical upstream face and $1:8$ downstream slope is proven, economical, and hydraulically stable for drops $> 0.9\text{ m}$.
2. Crest Design:
  • Crest length ($L$) = Bed width = $\mathbf{26.0\text{ m}}$
  • Discharge intensity: $$q = \frac{Q}{L} = \frac{15}{26} = \mathbf{0.577\text{ m}^3/\text{s/m}}$$
  • Head over crest ($H$) using standard Sarda equation: $$H = \left(\frac{q}{1.835}\right)^{2/3} = \left(\frac{0.577}{1.835}\right)^{2/3} = (0.3144)^{2/3} = \mathbf{0.463\text{ m} \approx 0.46\text{ m}}$$
  • Crest Level = $\text{U/S FSL} - H = 218.30 - 0.46 = \mathbf{217.84\text{ m}}$
  • Height of crest above u/s bed ($d$) = $217.84 - 216.50 = \mathbf{1.34\text{ m}}$
  • Crest Dimensions: $$\text{Top Width } (B_t) = 0.55 \sqrt{H + d} = 0.55 \sqrt{0.46 + 1.34} = 0.55 \sqrt{1.80} = 0.55 \times 1.342 = \mathbf{0.738\text{ m} \approx 0.75\text{ m}}$$ $$\text{Base Width } (B_b) = B_t + \frac{d}{8} = 0.75 + \frac{1.34}{8} = 0.75 + 0.168 = \mathbf{0.918\text{ m} \approx 0.92\text{ m}}$$
3. Cistern Design:
  • Length of Cistern ($L_c$): $$L_c = 5 \sqrt{H_L \cdot y} = 5 \sqrt{1.5 \times 1.8} = 5 \sqrt{2.70} = 5 \times 1.643 = \mathbf{8.22\text{ m} \approx 8.25\text{ m}}$$
  • Depression of cistern below d/s bed level ($x$): $$x = \frac{1}{4}(H_L \cdot y)^{2/3} = \frac{1}{4}(2.70)^{2/3} = 0.25 \times 1.939 = \mathbf{0.485\text{ m} \approx 0.50\text{ m}}$$
  • Cistern Bed Level = $215.00 - 0.50 = \mathbf{214.50\text{ m}}$
4. Impervious Floor Length (Bligh's Creep Theory, $C = 8$):
  • Maximum static seepage head = Drop $H_L = 1.50\text{ m}$
  • Total creep length required: $$L_{creep} = C \cdot H_L = 8 \times 1.50 = \mathbf{12.00\text{ m}}$$
  • Provide vertical cutoffs:
    • U/S cutoff depth $d_1 = 1.0\text{ m} \implies \text{vertical creep} = 2 \times 1.0 = 2.0\text{ m}$
    • D/S cutoff depth $d_2 = 1.5\text{ m} \implies \text{vertical creep} = 2 \times 1.5 = 3.0\text{ m}$
    • Total vertical creep = $2.0 + 3.0 = 5.0\text{ m}$
  • Horizontal floor length required: $$L_{floor} = L_{creep} - 5.0 = 12.00 - 5.00 = \mathbf{7.00\text{ m}}$$
  • Layout: Provide $2.5\text{ m}$ upstream floor and $8.25\text{ m}$ cistern floor: $$\text{Total provided horizontal floor} = 2.50 + 8.25 = \mathbf{10.75\text{ m}} > 7.00\text{ m} \quad (\mathbf{Safe})$$
